analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and natural gas based on carbon content to cut carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.headline: The first stand-alone federal carbon tax bill in decades never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in committee when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new federal tax on coal, petroleum, and natural gas, with the charge rising the longer it takes — starting at $3 per ton of coal in 1991 and reaching $15 per ton by 1995, alongside per-barrel and per-unit charges on oil and gas. The stated purpose was to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, the main driver of climate change. It was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the public would gain from reduced carbon dioxide emissions, since the tax makes carbon-heavy fuels more expensive relative to cleaner alternatives. Communities affected by coal pollution would also see less of it, because the tax hits coal hardest at $15 per ton. People who would be harmed by climate change — everyone, eventually — are the intended beneficiaries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, through lower carbon emissions

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax on the sale or importation of coal, petroleum, and natural gas based on their carbon content, with the explicit purpose of reducing carbon dioxide emissions
Sets the tax on coal at $15 per ton at full strength, the highest burden of the three fuels, so it falls most heavily on the most carbon-intensive fuel

Phases the tax in gradually starting January 1, 1991 — $3 per ton of coal, $0.65 per barrel of petroleum, and $0.08 per thousand cubic feet of natural gas in the first year — giving producers and consumers time to adjust
Applies the tax equally to imported fuels, so domestic producers are not put at a competitive disadvantage against foreign coal, oil, and gas

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers pay the tax directly — coal companies at up to $15 per ton, oil companies at up to $3.25 per barrel, and natural gas pipeline operators at up to $0.40 per thousand cubic feet. Because producers pass most excise taxes through to prices, households and businesses would pay more for electricity, gasoline, heating, and goods made with fossil energy. The bill directs the revenue nowhere in particular and provides no rebate or offset to soften the blow for consumers, so energy costs would rise across the board.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy consumers and fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises prices for gasoline, electricity, and heating fuel with no rebate, credit, or earmarking of the revenue, so the cost lands proportionally hardest on households that spend the largest share of their income on energy
A tax on inputs to nearly everything — electricity, transport, manufacturing — is mildly inflationary and would raise operating costs for energy-intensive industries and their workers
The bill contains no provisions to help coal-dependent regions absorb the shock, even though the coal tax at full strength is by far the largest of the three charges

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is straightforward and the gradual phase-in is sensible, but the design is bare-bones: it taxes carbon without returning the revenue, offsetting low-income households, or aiding coal communities, which is exactly the kind of gap that gave carbon taxes political trouble. The public benefit — slower accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere — is real but diffuse and long-term, while the costs are immediate and visible at the pump and the electric bill. A stronger version would have paired the tax with a consumer rebate or deficit reduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Pete Stark of California introduced the bill on May 10, 1990, as a standalone carbon tax on coal, petroleum, and natural gas
No representative joined as a cosponsor — the bill's cosponsor list is empty
The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax legislation, on the day of introduction
The committee took no further action, and the bill died there when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers are better off because the tax never took effect, and energy consumers pay no carbon charge today as a result of its failure. Thirty-plus years of delay in federal carbon pricing traces partly to bills like this one dying without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the carbon tax bill on May 10, 1990 and referred it to Ways and Means

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on the day of introduction

against.name: House members at large
against.what_they_did: Not one member of either party signed on as a cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the sponsor was a Democrat and the Democratic-led Ways and Means Committee let it sit.

industries.note: The bill taxes coal at $15 per ton at full strength — far above the petroleum charge of $3.25 per barrel — deliberately putting the heaviest burden on the most carbon-intensive fuel. The industry's interest in killing the bill ran directly against the public's interest in cutting emissions.

The bill adds up to $3.25 per barrel on petroleum and $0.40 per thousand cubic feet of natural gas, including on imports. Lower fossil fuel demand means less revenue for producers, though the phase-in gave them years to adjust.

Utilities and heavy industry would have passed the fuel tax through to customers in higher prices. They benefit from cheap fossil energy, which puts their interest against the emissions-reduction goal, though cleaner power sources would gain relative ground.
